title: Salesforce CRM OAuth Security Incident Response: APAC Playbook
summary: A practical Salesforce CRM OAuth security incident response playbook for APAC ops teams — token containment, log queries, notification clocks and vetting checklist.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Salesforce CRM OAuth incident response starts with blocking the connected app to revoke all its tokens, then inventorying tokens via the Tooling API, scoping access through Event Monitoring logs, sweeping exported Cases for embedded credentials, and assessing notification duties per jurisdiction.


---


Your CRM security perimeter does not end at your login page. It ends wherever the last third-party app you authorised stores its refresh token — which might be a startup's AWS account in Virginia, a vendor's CI pipeline, or a support engineer's laptop. That is the uncomfortable lesson of 2025, and it is why Salesforce CRM OAuth security incident response now belongs on the operations agenda, not just the security team's backlog. When Salesforce disabled the Klue Battlecards integration in November 2025 following an OAuth-related compromise, as reported by Salesforce Ben, no Salesforce vulnerability was exploited. A trusted token was. That distinction changes everything about how you prepare.


I run operations across Hong Kong, Singapore and the wider region, and I think about this the way I used to think about competition: you don't lose because the other side invented something new. You lose because you didn't cover the obvious gap. Connected apps are the obvious gap.


## What the Klue and Gainsight revocations actually tell us


Three incidents in 2025 followed the same shape. In August, Google Threat Intelligence Group attributed a campaign tracked as UNC6395 to the theft of OAuth tokens from the Salesloft Drift integration, affecting what Google described as a broad set of Salesforce customer instances — reporting at the time placed the figure in the hundreds of organisations. In November, Salesforce revoked tokens associated with Gainsight-published applications after detecting unusual activity, per Salesforce's own Help advisories. Weeks later, the Klue Battlecards integration was disabled.


The pattern is consistent:


- **No platform exploit.** The attacker authenticated as a legitimate connected app using a valid refresh token. From Salesforce's perspective, the traffic was authorised.
- **Bulk extraction via API.** Attackers ran broad SOQL queries against Account, Contact, Case, Opportunity and Attachment objects — exactly what an integration is permitted to do.
- **Secondary credential harvesting.** Google's reporting noted the attackers searched exported Case and support records for embedded secrets — AWS keys, Snowflake tokens, passwords pasted into support tickets. The CRM became a staging ground for the next breach.
- **Vendor-side origin.** The compromise happened in the vendor's environment. Your MFA, your IP restrictions, your session settings did not apply.


Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found third-party involvement in breaches doubled year over year to roughly 30% of cases, according to Verizon's own summary of the report's findings. Connected apps are the mechanism that makes that number real for CRM data specifically.


## The first 48 hours: an OAuth incident response playbook


Most teams searching for a Salesforce CRM OAuth security incident response template want something they can actually run during a bad Tuesday. Here is the sequence we recommend to operations leads, ordered by what buys you the most time.


*Related reading:*[CDP Build vs Buy Framework 2026: An APAC Buyer's Guide](https://branch8.com/posts/cdp-build-vs-buy-framework-2026)


### Hour 0–2: contain the token, not the user


Revoking a user's session does nothing if the refresh token lives with the vendor. Go to Setup → Connected Apps OAuth Usage, locate the app, and **block** it. Blocking revokes all tokens issued to that connected app immediately. Then revoke individual tokens if you need surgical control:


```text
1  -- Tooling API: inventory live tokens for a suspect app     2   SELECT   Id  ,   AppName  ,   AppMenuItemId  ,   UserId  ,   LastUsedDate  ,   UseCount  ,   DeleteToken    3   FROM   OauthToken    4   WHERE   AppName   =     'Suspect Integration'     5   ORDER     BY   LastUsedDate   DESC
```


```text
1  # Salesforce CLI: run the inventory against production    2  sf data query \    3    --query "SELECT AppName, UserId, LastUsedDate, UseCount FROM OauthToken ORDER BY LastUsedDate DESC" \    4    --use-tooling-api \    5    --target-org prod \    6    --result-format csv > oauth-tokens.csv
```


Keep the output. It becomes your evidence baseline.


### Hour 2–8: scope the blast radius


Your question is not "were we breached" but "what did that integration's service account have access to, and what did it actually read?" Pull the Event Monitoring logs. If you are on an edition without Event Monitoring, this is the moment you discover why it matters — and the reason I tell APAC operators to budget for it on any org holding regional customer data.


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus Analytics Monitoring in APAC: Beyond Dashboards](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-analytics-monitoring-apac)


*Related reading:*[Agentic Commerce Protocol ChatGPT Checkout: What APAC Retail Must Do](https://branch8.com/posts/agentic-commerce-protocol-chatgpt-checkout-apac-retail)


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus vs Adobe Ecommerce Stock: An APAC Operator's View](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-vs-adobe-ecommerce-stock-apac-decision)


*Related reading:*[LLM Hallucination Risk in APAC Workflows: A Procurement Guide](https://branch8.com/posts/llm-hallucination-risk-apac-workflows-procurement)


```text
1  SELECT   Id  ,   EventType  ,   LogDate  ,   LogFileLength    2   FROM   EventLogFile    3   WHERE   EventType   IN     (  'API'  ,     'RestApi'  ,     'BulkApi'  ,     'BulkApiRequest'  )     4      AND   LogDate   =   LAST_N_DAYS:  30     5   ORDER     BY   LogDate   DESC
```


Download the` API` and` BulkApi` logs and filter on the integration user ID from your token inventory. You are looking for row counts that spike beyond the integration's documented function. A battlecards tool reading 4,000 Opportunity records is normal. The same tool pulling every Case comment is not.


Cross-reference` LoginHistory` for the integration user and` SetupAuditTrail` for any permission changes in the window.


### Hour 8–24: hunt for secondary secrets


This is the step teams skip. Export the Case, Case Comment, Email Message and Attachment records the app could reach, and grep them for credential patterns. In the Salesloft Drift campaign, Google reported attackers specifically targeted these fields for` AKIA` prefixes, Snowflake connection strings and VPN credentials.


```text
1  # Pattern sweep over an exported case extract    2  grep -nEi "AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|xox[baprs]-|-----BEGIN (RSA|OPENSSH) PRIVATE KEY|snowflakecomputing\\.com" cases-export.csv
```


Anything that matches gets rotated, regardless of whether you can prove exfiltration. Rotation is cheap. Explaining to a regulator why you didn't rotate is not.


### Hour 24–48: notification assessment


Start the clock calculation now, not after forensics closes. More on regional timelines below.

## Queries that tell you who touched what


A good incident response example is really a good monitoring baseline run in anger. The same queries that scope an incident should run weekly when nothing is wrong.


**Connected app inventory with last use.** Any app with no activity in 90 days is a standing liability. Block it.


```text
1  SELECT   Name  ,   OptionsAllowAdminApprovedUsersOnly  ,   CreatedDate  ,   LastModifiedDate    2   FROM   ConnectedApplication    3   ORDER     BY   LastModifiedDate   DESC
```


**Integration users with excessive object access.** Pull the permission sets attached to every integration user and compare granted objects against the vendor's documented scope. In our experience auditing mid-market orgs across Hong Kong and Singapore, the most common finding is not a malicious app — it is an integration granted "Modify All Data" during a rushed implementation in 2021 that nobody ever narrowed.


**API call volume per connected app.** Set a threshold and alert on deviation. Transaction Security Policies in Salesforce Shield can block a session when a single query returns an unusual row count; even without Shield, a scheduled report on` EventLogFile` row counts catches the obvious cases.


For teams looking for a Salesforce CRM OAuth security incident response github starting point, the practical move is to version-control these queries alongside your deployment metadata, so the detection logic ships with the org rather than living in someone's notes app.


## Why APAC notification clocks make this harder


This is where regional operators get caught, and it is genuinely more complex than the US or UK picture.


If your CRM holds customer records across multiple APAC markets — which it almost certainly does if you sell regionally from a Hong Kong or Singapore hub — a single compromised connected app triggers several different obligations simultaneously:


- **Singapore.** Under the Personal Data Protection Act, the PDPC requires notification to the Commission no later than 3 calendar days after you assess a breach as notifiable, with affected individuals notified as soon as practicable. Notifiable generally means significant harm, or scale of 500 or more affected individuals, according to the PDPC's published data breach notification guidance.
- **Australia.** The OAIC's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requires assessment of a suspected eligible breach within 30 days and notification as soon as practicable once assessed, according to the OAIC's published scheme guidance.
- **Hong Kong.** The PCPD operates a voluntary breach notification regime under the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance — there is no statutory deadline, but the PCPD's published guidance recommends prompt notification, and reputational expectations in practice are much tighter than the law requires.
- **EU and UK data in an APAC org.** If any records belong to EEA or UK residents, GDPR's 72-hour clock applies regardless of where your instance sits.


The operational consequence: your incident response runbook needs a **data residency map per object** , built before an incident. When the Gainsight tokens were revoked, the companies that responded cleanly were the ones who could answer "which jurisdictions are in Contact?" in minutes rather than days. Those who couldn't spent their 72-hour window doing discovery.


For a global brand using Hong Kong or Singapore as an APAC operations hub, this is also a legitimate advantage. A regional hub that maintains a clean object-to-jurisdiction map and a tested revocation procedure can serve as the group's first responder for the whole region, instead of every market improvising.

## Vetting checklist before you click "Allow Access"


Procurement signs the contract. An ops manager clicks the OAuth consent screen. Those two events are usually weeks apart and involve different people, which is precisely the control gap.


Run every new Salesforce integration through this before authorisation:


**Scope and permissions**


- What OAuth scopes does the app request?` full` and` refresh_token` together is a standing key to your org. Push for` api` with a narrowly permissioned integration user instead.
- Which objects does the vendor's documentation say it reads? Create a dedicated integration user with a permission set limited to exactly those objects and fields — never a named human's credentials.
- Does it need write access at all? Most analytics and enablement tools do not.


**Vendor posture**


- Where are refresh tokens stored, and are they encrypted at rest with a customer-isolated key?
- Does the vendor hold SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001, and is the report current within 12 months?
- What is the vendor's own breach notification commitment to you, in hours? Put a number in the contract.
- Does the vendor sub-process your CRM data to other SaaS tools? Ask for the list.


**Operational controls on your side**


- Set the connected app policy to "Admin approved users are pre-authorized" so individual users cannot self-authorise apps.
- Apply IP relaxation and login hour restrictions to the integration user's profile where the vendor publishes static egress IPs.
- Enable API Access Control so only allowlisted connected apps can call your org at all. This single setting would have limited several 2025 incidents.
- Schedule a quarterly review of Connected Apps OAuth Usage with a named owner.


We worked with a multi-market beauty retail group running Salesforce alongside a regional service-centre operation, and the most valuable thing produced in that engagement was not a dashboard — it was a one-page authorisation gate that forced any new connected app through the same three questions before anyone touched the consent screen. Unglamorous. It is the operational equivalent of defensive positioning: boring until the moment it saves you.


## Who owns OAuth hygiene in a lean ops team?


In most APAC mid-market companies there is no dedicated SaaS security function. The Salesforce admin reports to sales ops, IT security looks after endpoints and network, and connected apps fall between them. That ambiguity is the actual risk.


My recommendation, based on how we staff and manage distributed operations teams across the region:


1. **Name a single accountable owner for connected app governance** — usually the Salesforce platform owner, not the CISO. They are the only person who sees the consent screens.
2. **Give them a 90-minute monthly slot** , calendar-blocked, to run the inventory queries and close out stale apps. Treat it like a training session: fixed, non-negotiable, measured.
3. **Define the escalation path before you need it.** Who can block a connected app at 2am Hong Kong time without waiting for a vendor's US business hours? If the answer is nobody, that is your highest-priority fix.
4. **Run one tabletop exercise per year** using a real incident as the scenario. "Salesforce just disabled an integration we rely on — go." Measure time-to-token-inventory and time-to-jurisdiction-list. Those two numbers predict how your real response will go.


The Reddit threads and admin forums that spiked during the 2025 incidents were full of the same question: *how do I even see which apps have tokens?* If your team cannot answer that in under ten minutes today, the governance problem is upstream of any tooling purchase.

## Preparing for the 2026 threat pattern


The direction of travel is clear enough. Attackers have learned that SaaS-to-SaaS trust is softer than the platforms themselves, and the CRM is the richest target in the stack because it concentrates customer identity, commercial context and — thanks to years of support tickets — other people's credentials. Expect the next wave to target integration marketplaces and the smaller vendors inside them, where security budgets are thinnest and a single compromise fans out across hundreds of orgs.


Salesforce has tightened its side: API Access Control, more aggressive token revocation, and faster customer advisories. The remaining variable is you. Effective Salesforce CRM OAuth security incident response in 2026 will be decided by work done in quiet weeks — a current connected app inventory, a jurisdiction map per object, a named owner with revocation authority, and a contract clause that forces your vendors to tell you fast. Teams in Hong Kong, Singapore and Sydney that build that muscle now will handle the next revocation notice as a Tuesday task rather than a crisis.
